clinicalPearls: Results from occlusion of the splenic artery or its branches, producing the classic wedge-shaped peripheral hypodense lesion on contrast-enhanced CT with its base against the capsule

Two dominant mechanisms are cardioembolic disease (atrial fibrillation, infective endocarditis, mural thrombus) and haematological disease (myeloproliferative neoplasms, sickle cell disease and massive splenomegaly of any cause)
In a young patient without a cardiac source, actively seek an underlying hypercoagulable state such as antiphospholipid syndrome or an inherited thrombophilia
Left upper quadrant pain radiating to the left shoulder tip (Kehr sign) reflects diaphragmatic irritation, but a large proportion of infarcts are clinically silent and found incidentally
In sickle cell disease repeated infarction causes autosplenectomy and functional hyposplenism; splenic infarction may also occur in sickle cell trait or HbSC disease at high altitude
Global rather than segmental infarction points to splenic artery or vein thrombosis, or to torsion of a wandering spleen
Most uncomplicated cases are managed conservatively with analgesia and treatment of the underlying cause, reserving intervention for complications
Complications to anticipate include splenic abscess, haemorrhage, subcapsular haematoma, pseudocyst formation and rupture
reference.pathophysiology: Splenic infarction occurs when arterial inflow through the splenic artery or its segmental branches is interrupted, causing ischaemic necrosis of the dependent parenchyma. Because the spleen has a largely end-arterial segmental supply, occlusion typically produces a wedge-shaped lesion with its base at the capsule. Emboli arising from the heart or aorta, in-situ thrombosis in hypercoagulable and myeloproliferative states, sickling and sludging of red cells within the microcirculation, mechanical compromise of the pedicle in a wandering spleen, or infiltration and expansion in massive splenomegaly can each precipitate ischaemia. Necrotic tissue may resolve with scarring and contraction, liquefy to form a pseudocyst, become secondarily infected to form an abscess, or bleed and rupture through the capsule.
additionalDifferentials: Left lower lobe pneumonia with pleuritic pain
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen to demonstrate the wedge-shaped perfusion defect and complications
Transthoracic and, if needed, transoesophageal echocardiography to seek a cardioembolic source
ECG and ambulatory monitoring for atrial fibrillation
Full blood count and peripheral blood film, with JAK2 and myeloproliferative screening where indicated
Thrombophilia and antiphospholipid antibody screen, particularly in younger patients
Blood cultures where infective endocarditis is suspected
Haemoglobin electrophoresis when a sickling disorder is possible
redFlags: Haemodynamic instability or peritonism suggesting splenic rupture and haemorrhage
Persistent swinging fever and rising inflammatory markers indicating abscess formation
An enlarging tender mass or falling haemoglobin from a subcapsular haematoma
New embolic phenomena elsewhere pointing to an untreated cardiac source
reference.prognosis: Uncomplicated splenic infarction usually settles with conservative management and its outlook is largely determined by the underlying disorder. Development of abscess, significant haemorrhage or rupture worsens the prognosis and may necessitate splenectomy.
pitfalls: Attributing left upper quadrant pain to pneumonia or pancreatitis and overlooking the infarct on imaging
Failing to pursue an embolic source or a myeloproliferative or thrombophilic cause
Missing an evolving abscess or rupture during conservative management
Overlooking resulting functional hyposplenism and the need for immunisation and infection prophylaxis
management: Supportive management of uncomplicated infarction with analgesia and hydration, as most settle conservatively
Identify and treat the underlying cause: anticoagulation for cardioembolic sources such as atrial fibrillation, and cytoreductive or disease-specific therapy for myeloproliferative neoplasms
Anticoagulate and investigate for a hypercoagulable state such as antiphospholipid syndrome or inherited thrombophilia in younger patients without a cardiac source
In sickle cell disease manage the sickling crisis with hydration, oxygenation and analgesia, and address precipitants such as hypoxia at altitude
Antimicrobial therapy with drainage or splenectomy if the infarct becomes secondarily infected, and operative management for significant haemorrhage or rupture
Surveillance imaging for complications such as abscess, pseudocyst or haemorrhage, and monitoring for functional hyposplenism
Immunisation and antibiotic prophylaxis where functional asplenia or autosplenectomy has occurred
